stims.text: Species as biological groups. Explain how variation within species and differences between species produce recognizable morphological or genetic clusters.
Species change and split. Explain why evolving populations and the splitting of lineages make species boundaries difficult to define.
Biological species membership. Use actual or potential interbreeding that produces viable, fertile offspring, together with reproductive isolation from other groups, to identify biological species.
A shared species gene pool. Explain how reproduction and migration spread alleles within a species and how restricted gene exchange permits populations to diverge.

Selecting usable species evidence. Select species evidence suited to the organisms and observations available: reproductive evidence for living sexual populations, or morphological, molecular, ecological, or ancestry evidence for strictly asexual organisms, fossils, or other cases where reproductive testing is unavailable.
Morphospecies identification. Use similarity in observable form to identify morphospecies.
Polymorphism. Recognize polymorphism as the occurrence of different phenotypes within one species.
Cryptic species. Recognize cryptic species as distinct species whose organisms look similar.
DNA barcode identification. Identify a specimen by matching a relevant DNA sequence to reference sequences associated with identified species.
Species maintained despite hybridization. Explain how selection against hybrids can maintain distinct species despite some genetic exchange.
Ecological niche. Describe an ecological niche as a species’ role and environmental and resource requirements.
Ecological species identification. Use ecological requirements to distinguish lineages, relating ecological differences to competition for resources when niches overlap.
Phylogenetic species identification. Use common ancestry, lineage membership, and shared lineage fate as evidence for a phylogenetic species grouping.
Timing of reproductive barriers. Classify a reproductive barrier as prezygotic when it acts before fertilization or postzygotic when it acts after fertilization.
Geographic isolation. Identify geographic isolation and explain how separation in space prevents reproductive encounters.
Ecological isolation. Identify ecological isolation and explain how different habitat use separates reproductive encounters.
Temporal isolation. Identify temporal isolation and explain how different reproductive times prevent reproductive encounters.
Behavioral isolation. Identify behavioral isolation and explain how differences in courtship signals or responses prevent mating.
Mechanical isolation. Identify mechanical isolation and explain how incompatible reproductive anatomy prevents mating.
Gametic isolation. Identify gametic isolation and explain how incompatibility between gametes or reproductive recognition interactions prevents fertilization.
Hybrid inviability. Identify hybrid inviability and explain how incompatible parental genetic contributions can prevent normal development.
Hybrid sterility. Identify hybrid sterility and explain how chromosome-pairing incompatibilities can prevent a viable hybrid from producing functional gametes.
Relatedness and genetic compatibility. Explain the chapter’s general relationship between closer genetic relatedness and less extreme reproductive incompatibility.
Reproductive costs and barrier timing. Explain how barriers before fertilization can avoid investment in embryos that would not produce fertile descendants.
Divergence leading to reproductive isolation. Explain how different mutations become fixed in separated populations, accumulating differences that can produce reproductive incompatibility.
Partial reproductive isolation. Recognize partial reproductive isolation as reduced hybrid viability or fertility between populations.
Subspecies. Recognize subspecies as differentiated geographic forms within a species, sometimes designated by an additional scientific-name term.
Allopatric and sympatric speciation. Classify speciation as allopatric or sympatric according to whether diverging populations were geographically separated or occupied the same area.
Dispersal and vicariance. Classify geographic separation as dispersal when organisms establish a distant population, or vicariance when a new barrier divides an existing population.
Peripatric speciation. Recognize a small peripheral population as a peripatric setting and explain how stronger drift and different selection pressures promote its divergence.
Adaptive radiation. Recognize rapid diversification from a common ancestor into ecologically different species and explain how ecological opportunity and population isolation promote it.
Co-speciation. Identify co-speciation and explain how splitting of a host lineage separates parasite populations that subsequently diverge.
Disruptive selection and sympatric divergence. Explain how selection against intermediate hybrids can counter the homogenizing effect of gene flow and allow populations in the same area to diverge.
Inferring geographic speciation history. Evaluate a proposed speciation history using geographic separation and genetic relationships, considering the populations’ locations during divergence.
Constraining speciation timing. Use the formation of a barrier or the age of an island to constrain a population’s possible history of separation or colonization.

Hybrid speciation. Identify hybrid speciation from a viable, reproducing hybrid lineage that is reproductively isolated from parental species, and explain how a distinct ecological role can support its persistence.
Auto- and allopolyploid origins. Classify a polyploid as autopolyploid when it originates within one species or allopolyploid when it originates through hybridization of different species.
Formation of a polyploid lineage. Explain how the joining of unreduced gametes can produce a polyploid lineage.
Genome doubling in plant evolution. Explain how the prevalence of even chromosome numbers supports a role for genome doubling in plant evolution.
Selection and speciation. Use the roles of drift and selection to explain how speciation can occur with or without natural selection and how selection can occur without speciation.

slots.topic: Species and speciation: Chapter 21 of Biology: How Life Works, fourth edition (2023). Undergraduate biology. Species criteria and their limits, reproductive barriers, mechanisms of speciation, and evidence about speciation history. Mutation, selection, drift, meiosis, and chromosome sets are supporting prior knowledge; teach their new connections to speciation within the selected target.

misconceptions.text: Individuals within a species must be identical, so variation within a group means it is not one species.
A geographic barrier immediately turns the separated populations into different species, even if they could still interbreed successfully.
Producing any hybrid offspring proves that the parents belong to the same biological species, even when the offspring are sterile.
Organisms that look alike must belong to the same species, and organisms that look different must belong to different species.
Any difference between two DNA sequences proves that the organisms are different species.
Failure to mate in a laboratory proves reproductive isolation, regardless of the testing conditions.
Recognizable species can never exchange genes; any hybridization must immediately erase the distinction between them.
Any difference in food choice is sufficient by itself to establish that two populations are separate species.
All organisms descended from any one common ancestor must be members of a single species.
Hybrid sterility is a prezygotic barrier because sterile offspring cannot fertilize eggs.
A hybrid that survives and grows normally must also be fertile.
Postzygotic barriers do not restrict gene flow because fertilization has already happened.
An existing population isolated by a newly formed barrier is an example of dispersal rather than vicariance.
Two related species living in the same place today must have originated by sympatric speciation.
Any gene flow makes genetic divergence and speciation impossible, no matter what happens to hybrids.
Every hybrid or organism with a new chromosome count is automatically a new species.
An autopolyploid necessarily originates from two species, and an allopolyploid necessarily originates within one species.
Natural selection is required for every speciation event and will always cause speciation whenever it acts.
Adaptive radiation means that one existing species simply grows to a large population size.
